Government Financial Position—Financial Statements for 6 Months Ended 31
December 2012
1. TODD McCLAY (National—Rotorua)  to the Minister of Finance : What
reports has he received on the Government’s financial position?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: I have received Treasury’s financial st atements for the 6 months to the end
of December. They show a $3.19 billion operating deficit before gains and losses for the
first 6 months of the financial year. That deficit is $158 million lower than forecast by
Treasury in its half-year update, primarily  reflecting lower expenditure than was
forecast. The Crown’s operating balance reco rded a surplus of $1.7 billion, which is
$2.3 billion higher than forecast. The result confirms that the Government is
maintaining a track to surplus through careful fiscal management.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What were the main factors behind the Government’s latest financial
results?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The statements show core Crown expenses at 0.8 percent
below forecast. Core Crown revenue is 0.1 percent below forecast. Lower expenditure
reflects moderate underspends across most departments, which total around $87 million,
with delay in two complex Treaty settlements until later in the year making up the
difference. Core Crown tax revenue was $31 million less than forecast, or 0.1 percent,
reflecting various overs and unders, including a higher than expected individual tax take
and higher source deductions associated wi th labour earnings growth. The operating
balance was boosted by invest ment gains from the New Zealand Superannuation Fund
and the ACC fund. The figures show that the Government is in control of new spending
and is getting better results from existing programmes.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What steps has the Government taken to manage its finances and get
back to surplus?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government has put spending and revenue initiatives
in place to balance the books. On the spending side, we have delivered two consecutive
Budgets showing zero net new expenditure, wh ile maintaining increases in health and
education spending. We have launched th e Better Public Services programme and
reprioritised $4.4 billion over 4 years to ensure New Zealande rs will see better results
without new resources. On the revenue si de, the Government has increased income
while improving the fairness of the tax system by shutting down loopholes. These
things include tightening the tax treatment  of property, increas ing GST, making it
harder for people to avoid paying tax through trusts, and making resources available for
the Inland Revenue Department to target tax avoidance.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What alternative proposals ha s he seen for managing the
Government’s finances?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have seen any number of alternative proposals. These
measures include putting a capital gains tax on every productive business and farm,
encouraging tax avoidance by increasing the gap between the top personal income and
company tax rates, discouraging all sorts of  private investment in the New Zealand
economy, printing money, and so on. That is  the Greens-Labour pr escription for the
New Zealand economy.
8004 Questions for Oral Answer 20 Feb 2013
Skycity, Convention Centre—Expressions of Interest Process
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Why did he say in June 2012 that “my office has had no
correspondence, no discussions, no involvement” in the c onvention centre process,
when he and his chief of staff dined with  the Skycity board on 4 November, he was
given a presentation that evening, and he urged them to think outside the box?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Quite simply, the question the me mber is asking about that I
answered was in relation to the expression of interest process. That was run by Mr
Brownlee at that point as the Minister. The poi nt that the member raises is quite right.
All of that was in the public domain. I myse lf said I had had dinner with Skycity. That
is all covered in part 1 of the report, and in part 1 of  the report the Deputy Auditor-
General says there are absolutely no issues at all. All of that was in the public domain.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that the Deputy Audito r-General found it was “not
appropriate” for the ministerial office staff to continue meeting with Skycity, why did
he allow his chief of staff to meet with Skycity executives five times, his deputy chief of
staff and the chief executive of the Departme nt of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to
also meet with Skycity, and himself to meet with Skycity twice—all immediately before
a supposedly open tender process?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Again, I would go through the process. Firstly, let us quote
from the report. The basic proposition the me mber is making is that there was some
cosy deal. The Deputy Auditor-General says: “We have seen no evidence to suggest that
the final decision to negotiate with SkyC ity was influenced by any inappropriate
considerations.” The Deputy Aud itor-General also says in the report that it is actually
quite normal and standard for Ministers a nd the Prime Minister to have discussions
with—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: That’s not what John Armstrong says.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, the member might not like it, because it does not suit his
narrative, but it is actually in the report if he  wants to read it. It is quite normal for that
to happen—nothing to see there. The situations the member has outlined all happened in
the exploratory phase. In part 1, the Deputy Auditor-General says there is nothing to see
there.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Was he warned by Gerry Brownlee on 1 March 2010 that “too many
people [were] talking to SkyCity,”; if so, wh y did his chief of staff, who promised to
“step back”, continue to meet with Skycity at least two more times?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What did happen at that time was that we were moving
beyond the feasibility stage to an  expression of interest. Wh at happened was that it was
logical, because there were a number of  Ministers involved—me as Minister of
Tourism, Mr Brownlee as Mi nister of Economic Developmen t, and other Ministers as
well, because there were a number of propos als. What ultimately happened is that it
made sense that, because what is now the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment would run that pr ocess, one Minister would ha ndle it. That is the way we
do things around here: quite often there are a number of Ministers involved, and in the
end there becomes a lead Minister. That is normal practice.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The essence of that
question was why his chief of staff met af ter the Brownlee warning. That was not
addressed.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thought—[ Interruption] Order! Order! [ Interruption] Order! It
would be helpful if I could make a ruli ng. I thought the questi on was satisfactorily
answered in that the Prime Minister talked  about it being a normal process. There were
a number of other proposals on the table at th at stage, and he felt it was quite normal
20 Feb 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8005
that his chief of staff and Ministers were involved in meeting potential proponents of
the convention centre in Auckland.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that his chief of  staff asked Skycity what  regulatory relief it
required in return for building the conventi on centre, was that question put to other
bidders; if not, does he consider that to be even-handed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There was an expression of inte rest process where, in fact, all
of those who decided to tender were told, actually, that th e Government was very cash-
strapped. Every deal was different in terms of the way it was negotiated. Skycity was in
a position where it was able, potentially, to go through a process where in return for
some concessions it was prepared to fully f und the process. In fact, this is the whole
debate, because—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Answer the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I am answering the questi on, Trevor. If you want me to
go through it, I can. If you want me to sit dow n, I am more than happy to do so. But if
you go through the process, pa rt 1, the exploratory ph ase—as the Deputy Auditor-
General says, nothing to see there. Part 3, the negotiations—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of  order, Mr Speaker. I wa s waiting for the answer to
this question. I actually asked whether the ot her bidders were offe red regulatory relief,
as Skycity received.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And the answer from the Prime Mi nister, in my mind, was quite
clear: all of those involved in the expression of interest process were advised that there
was a cash-strapped Government.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. With the greatest respect, I do
not want the answer to be in terpreted by you; I want the Prim e Minister to answer that
question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: With the greatest resp ect to you, sir, you are asking me to interpret
whether I think the Prime Minister has satis factorily answered your question and I was
doing that. The member has further supplementary questions if he wants to ask them.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. Your answer was that all
the bidders were told the Government is cash-strapped—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, that was not my answer. That  was the answer from the Prime
Minister.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: —and the question was whether all bidders were told that they
could get—or were they seeking—regulatory relief. If the Government is cash-strapped,
there is more than one response to being cash- strapped. It could be that they want a low
bid; it could be that they are seeking regulatory relief. So for the Prime Minister to
simply say the Government told all bidders that it was cash-strapped does not answer
the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: With respect, again, I have judged that the Prime Minister has, to
my satisfaction, answered the question. Th e Leader of the Opposition has further
supplementary questions if he wants to delve into the answer by the Prime Minister, and
that is the way it should happen. It is not for members to take points of order to continue
to dispute an answer that is given, if I have ruled that it is satisfactory.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given his chief of staff asked Skycity what regulatory relief it
required, was regulatory relief offered to the other bidders on the convention centre?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, regulatory relief has not  been offered to Skycity. That
may be part of the negotiations  that they want, but, actually, all bidders were told that
we were looking for creative solutions a nd it was a cash-strapped Government. Every
bid was different. In fact, in the case of ev ery bid, with the excep tion of Skycity, they
were asking the Government for $300 million - odd to build it.
8006 Questions for Oral Answer 20 Feb 2013

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he saying that his chief of st aff did not offer Skycity, or did not
ask it if it wanted, regulatory relief, or not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What I am saying is that no agreement has been reached with
Skycity, although we hope one w ill be. But what is quite cl ear is that in the early
exploratory stages where we had discussions with Skycity, I told them myself “Think
creatively and see what deal you can come up with.” At that point, after we had done
that, which was all in phase one, for which the Deputy Auditor-General says there is
nothing to see, everything is totally fine, and that is OK, we went to an expression of
interest process. What the Deputy Auditor-General does not like about that process is
that she says—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [ Interruption] I am sorry, but I
have been very patient. The question I asked was: did his chief of staff ask or offer
Skycity regulatory relief? It is simple.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think that the Prime Minister certainly moved to the extent of
saying that he himself offered regula tory relief. It would be helpful—[ Interruption]
Order! Order! I am trying to ru le. It would be helpful if the Prime Minister was able to
answer in respect of the chief of staff.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That may well be the case—that that is the proposal. But this
is the whole point—the proposal of the deal  to Skycity was one where we said to
Skycity “If you want to come up with a pr oposal, the Government’s  preferred position
is no cash. Come up with a range of options.”  In fact, what the Deputy Auditor-General
says is that having gone through five people in  the expressions of interest, what they
were unable to do—the officials at that po int—was to advise the Government what
actually would be on the table. That is wh at took the extended period of time. The
Deputy Auditor-General believes that we should have truncated discussions—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. I am so rry to keep doing this,
but I just want a simple answ er to a very simple question:  did his chief of staff offer
Skycity regulatory relief? It is simple.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The right honourable Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The simple answer is that I am sure the chief of staff reiterated
my comments, which were to think laterally, of which that  might be a possibility, and
that has been the basis of the whole deal. Th at is the point, is it not—to come up with
some proposals and we will have a look. The problem with the whole issue was that
actually we have been unable to actually assist—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The right honourable Prime Minist er—the Rt Hon Winston Peters,
a point of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Given who is there
now, anyone could have the job. My point is this: the Prime Minister is being asked a
simple question, and he is refusing to answer  it. Thinking laterally is not the answer.
Did he or did he not, or his chief of staff, engage in that arrangement? That is what he is
being asked.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And the Prime Minister’s answer at the start was he is sure that his
chief of staff repeated the same sorts of offe rs that the Prime Minister had made to all
the bidders about being expansive with their ideas.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: That is not the question. The question is: was there a
special offer made? Not to think laterally, but the offer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That was not the question. The question has now very
definitely been satisfactorily answered—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Was the answer yes or no?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The answer was he was sure that his chief of staff repeated
statements very similar to the Prime Minist er’s. If members bothe red to listen to the
20 Feb 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8007
question and to the answers, I am sure we would have far fewer points of order about
the quality of answers.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that he told Skycity th at the Government was providing no
capital funds for the conventi on centre, did he provide the same information to other
bidders; if not, does he consider this to be even-handed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is actually quoting me  incorrectly. I said that the
Government’s preferred position was no cash in put. Yes, that was made clear to other
businesses that that the Government was cash-strapped and that that was preferred. Yes,
it was made clear through the e xpression of interest process that other tenderers should
put up the best proposal they could. One happened to put up a public-private
partnership, which meant the Government  paid over a long period of time, one
happened to put up regulatory changes, and others basically put up a proposal where we
paid for it.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: At what point in his interactions  with Skycity was he told that
Skycity wanted additional pokie machines as a condition for funding its convention
centre?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am sure that would have occurred when the officials came
back at the end of phase two and said to  the Ministers: “We think you should accept the
Skycity proposal. It would require these sorts of changes, which would then have to be
negotiated in part 3.”, which is what we are doing at the moment.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: At what point did the Prime Minister come to understand that the
condition of Skycity’s bid was that there be more pokie machines made available to
them?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That cannot be confirmed becau se we actually do not have a
deal with it, and it may well come up with a variety of different proposals. But in 2009,
when I had the dinner with Skycity and said to  think laterally, of course I assumed that
they would want to have more pokie machines  or an extension of their licence. By the
way, that is exactly what Labour did in 2002.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: What discussions were he  and his staff involved in
regarding the planned location of the Skycity conve ntion centre on land owned not by
Skycity but by New Zealand taxpayers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I cannot detail the ex act ones, but what was clear was that if
Skycity was to build a larger convention centr e than the original one they wanted, at
some point I was aware that they would n eed to acquire land. That land was owned by
Television New Zealand (TVNZ).

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How did Skycity conclude it had access to taxpayer-owned
TVNZ State-owned asset land if he did not do a secret side-deal in favour of his mates
at the casino on that issue?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is pretty straightforward. Skycity, after it decided it would
be prepared to enter an expression of interest process to have a larger convention centre,
went off to its architects. It s architects designed such a thing, realised they needed more
land, worked out who owned the land, and approached Television New Zealand.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If that is true, how come Television New Zealand and its
board had no awareness of that, but Skycity did, and is it not true that he promised
Skycity that his Government would privatise TVNZ’s assets—[ Interruption] Well, you
can laugh, but the board has no knowledge. At the time I am talking about, it had no
knowledge of this, so Gerry can laugh all he  likes, embarrassingly, I might say. But the
fact is there was a secret side-deal—is it not true, Prime Minister—in favour of Skycity,
in favour of his mates, and how sleazy is that?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Rt Hon Prime Minister, probably with no reference to the latter
part of the question.
8008 Questions for Oral Answer 20 Feb 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I cannot speak for the Television New Zealand board, but I am
finding it reasonably hard to believe that Television New Zealand entered a commercial
agreement with Skycity to sell land that it owned, and it did so without its board
knowing. If that happened, then maybe its board process needs to be improved, and
maybe the mixed-ownership model would work for it. But contrary to what the member
says, we have no plans to sell it or enter it into the mixed-ownership process.
Skycity, Convention Centre—Expressions of Interest Process
3. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by his reported statement that “anyone expecti ng details of a ‘cosy so rt of little deal’
would be disappointed” by the Deputy Aud itor-General’s report into the SkyCity
Convention Centre negotiations?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, absolutely. The Deputy Auditor-
General’s report examines all th ree stages of the process to date, and concludes that the
initial exploratory and feasibility stage, wh ich was the stage I was involved in, and the
third stage, the current negotiations that the member is asking about, were entirely
appropriate. The report noted some procedural issues, primarily that officials did not do
enough planning, which I understand the mini stry has taken on board, and that the
assessment of the expression of interest pr ocess went on too long; however, as the
Deputy Auditor-General said in the report and made qu ite clear, the substantive
outcome would not be different . That is why the central finding of the report—and the
basic accusation that that member has made  and why she owes me an apology—is that
there is no evidence to suggest that the final deal—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. That answer went on far too
long. It was a straightforward question. [ Interruption] It was a straightforward question.
We on this side of the House were allowing time for the Prime Minister to answer in
full, but that, I think, undid th e patience of the House. I w ould ask you to make sure he
does not do it again.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It undid the patience of the member, I accept that. It was a very long
answer. It was a very full answer.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. While the co-leader of
the Greens was making her point of order th ree Government front-bench Ministers,
three in the second row, and six backbenchers interjected—at least.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member for his assistance. As was mentioned yesterday,
points of order should be hear d in silence. If they are not , then we get the sort of
disorder that we are experiencing today, so I request the cooperation of all members for
points of order to be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Can the Prime Minister confirm th at he made that statement hours
before the Deputy Auditor-General releas ed her report into the pokies for the
convention centre deal?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That may well be right. I cannot  remember the exact time. It
was probably Monday at my post-Cabinet pre ss conference, which takes place at about
4 o’clock. The report was released, I think, at 2 o’clock, so I guess it was 22 hours.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I seek leave to table a document, a transcript of a Radio New Zealand
interview—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, we are—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: —that is not publicly available.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is publicly available. [ Interruption] Order! The member will
resume her seat. We discussed only yester day, when I elaborat ed on the tabling of
20 Feb 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8009
documents, that we are not tabling transcri pts from radio interviews. They are freely
available to members if members want to search for them.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: No they’re not.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes they are.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member disputing my ruling, because my patience is getting
particularly thin today.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member disputing my ruling?

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: No. Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member about to dispute my ruling?

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: No. Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Then I will hear the point of order.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Yesterday you did clarify the tabli ng of documents. You did say that
old reports could be tabled, and that info rmation that was not publicly available or
widely publicly available could also be tabled. If you had given me the chance to
explain, this is a transcript that is not publicly available. Even if it was reported
yesterday, it still meets the criteria—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Then the member—[ Interruption] Order! The member will
resume her seat. The member is now dispu ting my ruling and, if she continues to do
that, I will ask the member to leave the House. [ Interruption] Order! If the member
continues—[Interruption] Order! Otherwise we will be having somebody with early
showers. The member is disputing my ruling. What I also said yesterday was that we
would table documents that I f eel are useful to the debate in the House. If members are
keen enough to discover that tr anscript, then they have the ability to go back to their
offices and do so. I will not be putting the leave.

items.speaker: Rt Hon John Key
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. Just speaking to your ruling,
Mr Speaker, that was a transcript of Morning Report , which will be available on the
Radio New Zealand website. It is freely available everywhere.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And so I have ruled.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I do not want to litigate this
specific issue. I would like to ask you, Mr Speaker, whether ther e was an opportunity
for you to consider the wider issue of radio transcripts, because, in the case of radio
transcripts, it is often possible to purchase them. Ministers have them available, because
they can purchase them. Opposition members ca nnot purchase them, and, therefore, we
have to either have our staff transcribe them, which is quite a resource-intensive
exercise, or, once it has already been transc ribed by someone, get it from someone else.
So can I ask you to consider it further—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I will consider it further for the benefit of the member and for
the House.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Prime Minister aware that  the Office of the Auditor-General
expected that report to be treated in the strictest confidence becau se of concerns about
market sensitivities, and that no one other than Ministers, Skycity, and the Office of the
Auditor-General had access to that report before 2 p.m. yesterday?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am well and truly aware that  there was an embargo, but, as
we know—for instance, last Friday I read re ports of characterisation of Shane Jones’
Auditor-General’s report. The comments that I made, of someone claiming a cosy sort
of little deal, are hardly market sensit ive, and, as the member knows, her basic
accusation and claim to the A uditor-General was as follows—because maybe she needs
reminding of it—that somehow, the main que stion underlining the inquiry was whether
the Government’s decision—
8010 Questions for Oral Answer 20 Feb 2013

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. This is not an answer to my
question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I did answer it directly—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is attempting to answer your question, but if
the member continues to ask questions and then rises to her feet through the answer, she
is not going to hear the answer to the question she has asked.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY

Christchurch, Recovery—Criteria for Offer on Vacant Red Zone Land
4. DENIS O’ROURK E (NZ First)  to the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake

items.speaker: Recovery
items.text: What criteria did he use in deciding th at owners of vacant sections in the red
zone of Christchurch should only be compensa ted at half of the sections’ most recent
rateable value?
There has been no decision to compensate the owners of vacant land in the red zones in
Christchurch. There has, rather, been an offer to purchase that vacant land in those red
zones, and that offer has been made to the owners of those propert ies. The criteria for
determining the offer were in relation to the original red zone offer to insured
homeowners in those areas, where we sought to give those people certainty, simplicity,
and confidence moving forward. The plan was to get those families in the worst-
affected areas into positions where they could move on with their lives. By very
definition, people who own vacant land are not living on it.
Denis O’Rourke : I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. The question was very
specific in asking about the criteria for valuing the compensation offered by way of
offer, which was only half of the rateable va lue. I do not believe th at question actually
was answered. All sorts of ot her things were said, but th ere was no actual information
about the criteria that led to a 50 percent offer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question was around compensation, and the Minister started his
answer by saying they are not offering compen sation; they are offering to purchase. He
then went on to say that th e two criteria that were impor tant were the opportunity to
give certainty to those people with that la nd, and confidence to move forward. I would
have thought that adequately answered  the question. The member has further
supplementary questions.
Denis O’Rourke: Given that it is standard practice to pay full market value when the
Government compulsorily acquires private land, why was fair and established practice
not followed when, effectively, compulsor ily purchasing red zone vacant sections,
irrespective of whether there is any land damage or not; or is the Government just
taking advantage of a disaster situation to get the land on the cheap?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Firstly, I refute many of the allegations and inferences
in the member’s question. But wh at I will say is this: if he  wants to insist that the
Government pay market valuation for those sections, he does not  do those people any
good at all. We had a valuation conducted on 4,136 properties on 30 June 2012, and the
result of that was that the market va lue assessed for those properties was $2,600 per
property. If he wants to get the map, good luck with his crusade. I want to be more
generous, and give them 50 percent of the 2007 valuation.

Skycity, Convention Centre—Potential Economic Benefits
5. KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What economic opportunities will a new convention centre bring for
Auckland?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is estimated that
the proposed Auckland convention centre w ould generate very significant economic
benefits, including a $90 million annual inje ction into the Auckland economy, an
estimated 1,000 jobs during construction, and 800 jobs once it is  up and running. Of
course, the overall economic benefits of the proposal will be assessed before the
Government will proceed, and of course we want a good deal for taxpayers. But there is
no question that an internati onal-size convention centre is essential for New Zealand if
we are to tap into the growing market of valu able business visitors that we are currently
missing out on.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What support has he seen for the proposed new
convention centre in Auckland?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have seen very widespread support. For example, I have
seen a report from Martin Snedden, who h eads the Tourism Industry Association, who
said: “Development of a world-class convention centre will not only create a major new
market for our tourism industry, it will c ontribute significantly to New Zealand’s
economic recovery,”. I have seen a report fr om the Holiday Parks Association of New

items.speaker: Zealand that said
items.text: “A world-class convention centre will provide a real boost for holiday
parks, New Zealand’s tourism industry and the country’s economy,” . Michael Barnett,
from the Auckland chamber of commerce, said: “the SkyCity proposal to fund and build
a purpose built national convention centre in central Auckland is a game changer.” And,
of course, there is the backing that one Helen Clark gave to a similar deal to this current
Skycity convention centre proposal. That deal involved far less investment than is being
proposed now, in return for an additional 230 pokie machines.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: Is he aware of any opposition to the proposed new
convention centre in Auckland?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have seen some opposition to  the proposal, just as I have
seen opposition to a number of the hands- on decisions made by this Government to
encourage jobs in the New Zealand economy, which is, at the very least, a little ironic.
Some organisations have consistently opposed  new convention centres, but others have
a more confusing history. For example, the l eader of one organisation said in 2004, in
relation to a similar project: “Here in New Zealand it has been pleasing to see
continuing investment in the quality of our  tourism infrastructure. In Auckland, Sky
City has pumped $140 million into its new C onvention Centre,”. Yet the current leader
of the same organisation today supposed ly vehemently opposed this proposal. That
organisation is, of course, the very confused New Zealand Labour Party.

Welfare Fraud—Deterrents
7. MIKE SABIN (National—Northland)  to the Associate Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What steps is the Government taking to reduce welfare fraud?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.role: Associate Mi nister for Social Development

items.text: Today I announced new measures to prevent,  detect, and deter welfare fraud. We know
that the vast majority—more than the vast majority—of the 340,000 beneficiaries in this
country are honest and follow the rules, but fraud, even from a small minority, is
unacceptable. That is why the Government is equipping the Ministry of Social
Development with the ability to target high-value fraud to pr event reoffending by
known fraudsters and to recover money that is  taken faster. These ch anges will help us
ensure that the welfare system is there to support the needy and not  be taken advantage
of by the greedy.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: How much money is lost to welfar e fraud each year, and what effect
will these changes have on that loss?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: A small minority who rip off the welfare system cost
the taxpayer a sizable amount of money. Last  year 714 people were convicted of fraud
totalling over $23 million. A further $18 milli on was taken by dishonest overpayments
where there was insufficient evidence to prosecute. These changes will help us stop that
money going out the door in the first place an d to recover what is taken even faster.
They aim to deliver on the Government’s el ection commitment to catch, prevent, and
recover $200 million worth of welfare fraud over the next 4 years.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: How will these new measures prevent reoffending by known welfare
fraudsters?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Three-quarters of the people we caught last year who
were taking money they were not entitled to had previously b een investigated for
potential welfare fraud. Even though we know these people have been dishonest before,
too many of them end up reoffending. Startin g this year these people will find their
future interactions with Work and Income  subject to greater scrutiny, and we will
restrict their access to self-service options and place a higher bar for them to prove that
they are not trying to rip off the taxpayer again. Although they wi ll still receive what
they are entitled to, there will be strong barri ers in place to stop them from taking more
than that again.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Would some honourable member care  to move that the House take
note of miscellaneous business?

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I apologise to members, but I think there was an urgent debate you might have
to rule on.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do apologise, Mr Mallard. I have  received a letter from Grant
Robertson seeking to debate under Standi ng Order 386 the repo rt from the Deputy
Controller and Auditor-General on the Skyc ity convention centre. The release of the
report is a matter of recent oc currence. As an Auditor-Gen eral’s report there is no
ministerial responsibility for the report itself, though I do accept that it deals with
matters involving ministerial responsibility.
The test for whether a particular case re quires the immediate a ttention of the House
is a high one. The report finds no evidence that the final decision to negotiate with
Skycity was influenced by any inappropriate consideration, but it raises some process
concerns. There must be an element of urge ncy for a matter to take precedence over
other business. Working through the concerns raised may take some time. The purpose
of an urgent debate is to hold the G overnment accountable for its decisions. The
Government is accountable for the concerns raised, but this is an ongoing matter. To
8022 Urgent Debates Declined 20 Feb 2013
warrant an urgent debate being held, ther e must be a new situ ation or decision of
importance in itself. Good prac tice for public sector purchas ing is important to public
confidence and our system of government, but I am not convinced that the matters have
reached the point where I would be justified in setting aside the business of the House
today. There are other occasions on which this matter can be debated. The application is
therefore declined.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business. Yesterday we had the announcement of the Deputy Auditor-
General’s report on the Skycity  deal, and the Prime Minister  said that he was totally
vindicated by this report. Everybody who ha s read this report,  any reasonable New
Zealander, will see that he was not vindicate d; he was implicated. He was implicated
right up to his eyeballs. This was a shonky deal, and Mr Key is donkey deep in a shonky
deal. He was seen to be pulling the strings right  up to the last minute. It is a litany of his
involvement in ensuring that Skycity got th e best deal. It was ensuring that his mates
got in front of the process.
Let us just look at how this litany started. In 2009 John Key advised himself—as you
do, of course—to chase Skycity for a deal to build a national convention centre. Then he
was not sure about ensuring that his own people and his own staff would make sure that
that deal was nailed down and sealed, because he met with the Skycity bosses in May
2009. But he cannot remember exactly what wa s discussed—but that is what happens.
We do have brain fade in this Chamber, and that was what happened.
On 24 August he wrote on a brie fing note that he wanted the Skycity deal closed off.
In September his chief of staff, his deputy chief of staff, and the head of the Department
of the Prime Minister and Cabinet met with Skycity to go over the plans. In September a
senior tourism official told them that S kycity wanted its gambling licence extended for
building the centre—it gets worse and worse. Then in November John Key and Wayne
Eagleson had a cosy little dinner with Skycity bosses so they could look at the plans and
“think outside the box”. On 3 December 2009 the Department of the Prime Minister and
Cabinet warned John Key about the dodgy proce ss in a private briefing note, but he
does not care—he does not care. He does not need to care, because his chief of staff was
still going on and on meeting with Skycity and seeing what it wanted for this little deal.
On 23 December 2009 the chair of Skycity wrote to John Key telling him of the
regulatory reforms he wanted. What were th ey? What were those regulatory reforms?
Well, more pokies. They were more pokies and an extension to Skycity’s gambling
licence. In other words, the problem gamb lers of New Zealand are stumping up the
money for this convention centre in a dodgy de al that no other bidder gets to have a
look at. In fact, no bidder othe r than Skycity gets to know that actually the Government
is not going to put up any of the money. No  other bidder actuall y knew that; only
Skycity knew that. Only Skycity gets to be offered regulatory reforms in the form of
some sweet deal that John Key offers to it.
This is a shonky deal. It is a deal that should not be allowed in a country like New
Zealand. John Key is involved up to  his eyeballs in a shonky d eal. It is a deal that John
Armstrong calls something that you would expe ct from a “banana republic without the
bananas”. That is a disgrace to this House.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Ah! The only
problem with that observation from the pro tem leader of the Labour Party is that it is all
rubbish. Firstly, the Deputy Auditor-General  made it clear that there is nothing—
nothing at all—to suggest that the final decision to negotiate with Skycity was
influenced by any inappropriate  considerations. The report says that a great deal of
20 Feb 2013 General Debate 8023
careful work was undertaken by officials to understand the market and that the officials
were acting in good faith, and it stresses that any issues were procedural rather than
about the substance of what was being consider ed. So that is the first problem with the
Opposition’s opposition to this proposed deal.
There are two other problems with the Opposition’s opposition to this particular deal,
and the first one is political history, because  despite its virulent opposition—its virulent
opposition—to the proposal that is in front of  us, it did the same thing not 10 years ago.
In fact, the former Prime Minister “St Helen of Mt Albert”, Helen Clark, actually said in
respect of the previous S kycity convention centre poker -machine deal: “Here in New
Zealand it has been pleasing to  see continuing investment in  the quality of  our tourism
infrastructure. In Auckland, Sky City has pumped $140 million into its new Convention
Centre,”. And the tourism Minister of the da y, Mark Burton, said that the investment
“will give it the capacity to compete for a whole new range of prestige events. The
potential gains from this are widespread—not only for Skycity, but for the Auckland
city and region, the tourism industry, and th e whole of New Zealand.” This was the
Labour Party not 10 years ago. Today the La bour Party is a ne w Labour Party that
wants nothing to do with those sorts of arrangements.
The interesting thing—and the second problem  Labour has—is that this is supposed
to be the new “hands-on” Labour Party that is supposedly interested in rolling its
sleeves up and making hands-on approaches  to Government. Well, not today—not
today. Today it is hands-off. Today the chief whip of the Labour Party was on the radio
saying: “The market should pr ovide. We shouldn’t get involved in regulatory deals for
Skycity convention centres. It is the market that should provide.” That was Mr Hipkins
just this morning as he repudiated the new “hands-on” approach of the Labour Party.
But it was only today that it was hands-off—really! Well, apart from with The Hobbit.
With The Hobbit Labour was also hands-off. It did not want any law changes to allow
the Hobbit films to be done here.
It is also hands-off on resource manageme nt law changes. So  Labour is hands-on
except for resource management and for The Hobbit , and it is also hands-off for the
Auckland convention centre.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: And job creation.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: And job creation. Yes, it is hands-off there. It is hands-off
for oil and gas exploration. It does not want anything to do with any law changes there.
But apart from that it is very hands-on. Well, except for Bathurst Resources at the
Denniston Plateau. It is hands-off about that, but that  is just an exce ption. It is also
hands-off about aquaculture investment. Yes, indeed, it is hands-o ff about that. Apart
from that it is hands-on. Oh no, actually, no. It is hands-off. It does not want any
international investment. It does not want any increase in irri gation or intensification of
agriculture. It is hand s-off there too. But apart from that it is hands-on, which means
that it is hands-on only in one way, and that  is hands on your wallet. That is the only
way the Labour Party is hands-on: it is hands on the taxpayers’ wallet. That is its
solution to every problem. It would roll out the cheque book, raise the debt, and get the
Greens to print the money. That would be the solution.
So today we have learnt that Labour’s “ha nds-on” slogan is rubbish. We have learnt
that it has a new hypocrisy about what it di d 10 years ago. We have learnt that the
Opposition leader is grasping at  straws with an Office of the Auditor-General report
that, frankly, says that there were only some  procedural issues and that the substantive
result would not have been changed. That is the quality of the Government’s opposition
today.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: There is no way that the Government can claim
vindication from this report. This is anot her tawdry example of low standards by a
8024 General Debate 20 Feb 2013
Government that does the opposite of what it says it will do. It was elected with John

items.speaker: Key saying
items.text: “I expect high standards from  my Ministers. If they don’t meet the
standards I set, then, obviously, I will take action if necessary.”—except when it is him.
Time after time we have got low standards from this Prime Minister, whether it is the
teapot tapes and using the police against the media during the election; whether it is the
Dotcom affair, where he had brain fades a nd denied having received information about
Dotcom, because it was embarrassing for the li ne he was running; or whether it is the
spin that he is now putting on this report from the Deput y Auditor-General in respect of
Skycity.

items.speaker: The Office of the Auditor General says
items.text: “we do not consider that the approach
adopted was appropriate. The result was that  one submitter was treated differently from
the others during the evaluation process.” And what are the consequences worth?
Millions and millions of dollars and, of course, terrible social harm from gambling.
The Deputy Auditor-General’s report show s that officials we re worried. On 12
November a ministry official emailed the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
summarising where the process was at, noting that Treasury had advised that ministry
officials should seek advice from the Auditor-General to determine the probity of the
current process with Skycity. The Deputy Auditor-General sa ys it was emailed to the
Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
What does the Prime Minister say today? Oh, no record of it being found on their
side. That is just not credible, because do you know what? Some days later we had a
personal note sent to the Prime Minister. I will read what the Deputy Auditor-General
says for this: “The Treasury’s comments were referred to in a 12 November 2009 email
from a Ministry official to DPMC and incl uded in a private DPMC  briefing note to the
Prime Minister on 3 December 2009.”
What did he do today in respect of being as ked about that note, about that reminder?
He obfuscated. He did not answer the question. He denied, effectively, taking
responsibility for the fact that the officials were worried, the offici als were concerned,
the officials were warning the ministry, Tr easury had been alerte d to it, Treasury was
worried and raised it with the Prime Minister, and the Department of the Prime Minister
and Cabinet raised it to the Prime Minister  again. Still the Prime Minister ignored it.
And he pretends he comes here with clean hands.
It is just as incredible as his earlier denials of responsibility around involvement with
Dotcom, his refusal to read the other things  involving Skycity again, on that occasion
with Mr Banks in respect of the donations saga, which was plainly illegal. The Prime
Minister is not worried about it. It is banana republic stuff, as John Armstrong said in
the New Zealand Herald . It is disgraceful conduct. It is the slippery slope towards
corruption.
In Auckland business people are worried about it. When this happened, before this
report came out, I had approaches from am ongst the most senior business people in
Auckland, who were saying it was not fair. It was not fair that a secret deal is done with
Skycity showing that regulatory holidays are available, worth millions and millions of
dollars, and that they are not shown as pot entially available to other tenderers who
might be interested, or other people who mi ght be interested in building a convention
centre. It is disgraceful cronyism.
It is on the back of the Prime Minister ha ving Mr McElrea, his electorate chair, on
the Broadcasting Commission, also known as New Zealand On Ai r. It is on the back of
the teapot tapes saga. No standard is t oo low for this Government. We are sliding
towards being a banana republic in respect of these sorts of issues.
This is the Government that is pretendi ng to make amendments to improve fiscal
responsibility when it will not even adhere to the standards of decency, openness, and
20 Feb 2013 General Debate 8025
transparency, which we have long held to in New Zealand, and which we should strive
to uphold every day. This sorry saga does not reflect well on the Government or the
Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: What a fantastic start to the year this
John Key - led National Government has had—what a fantastic start. As much as the
Opposition might want to scrape the bottom of the barrel and throw accusations and
mud around this House, this Government is delivering for New Zealanders, and, what is
more, New Zealanders know it. In the last two public polls that we have had in the last
week, what have we seen? We have seen 49 percent support for National in Television
One’s poll, and, what, 45 percen t in Fairfax’s. Actually, it is around about the election
result at the end of 2011. In fact, that show s that New Zealanders think that no matter
how much the Labour Opposition and its colleagues the Greens might like to come to
this House, be nasty, and throw accusations  around that have no substance in fact—no
substance in fact—the people of New Zealand actually do not give a toss what they say,
whether inside the House or not. They can s ee that this Government is getting on with
doing things that actually matter to everyday New Zealanders.
We had the Prime Minister’s announcement at the beginning of the year of the
increase in and reorganisati on around apprenticeships, and that went down well out in
provincial New Zealand, I can tell you. Then the Prime Minister came to this House and
made his annual statement, and that was well received. That showed New Zealanders
that the National-led Government has a stro ng plan, that it is focused on its four
priorities, and that it knows that it is slow  and steady as she goes. No rinky-dinky silver
bullets are going to make this economy s uddenly start up, and printing money is not a
good idea.
I want to take just a few minutes to talk about two portfolios that I have
responsibility for that have had an enormous start to the year 2013. So far this year we
have announced, first of all, that we are tu rning three prisons into  working prisons, to
make sure that prisoners get increased oppor tunities for employment training. So that
means structured 40-hour weeks for prisone rs working inside those prisons, getting
good work experience, getting good qualificat ions, and having a better chance of not
reoffending when they leave prison.
We have talked about the increase in polic e foot patrols. There is an average 70
percent increase across New Zealand in po lice out on the beat in their communities—
visible, preventing crime, and deterring cr ime from happening. The Prime Minister and
I launched last week the delivery to our po lice of expert technology that they should
have had years ago. You have  to wonder what the Labour Party did with all those
surpluses that it had. Labour did not equip our modern police with  modern technology,
but this Government is suppor ting them with the roll-out of technolo gy. That roll-out
will mean an extra half a million front-line policing hours every year available for crime
prevention.
Last week I opened in Christchurch the new police station. That is a first in this
country, because we have Police and the Department of Corrections working together in
the same building. That was an enormous ask and a significant event not just for
Christchurch but also for the justice sector. Corrections and Police are working together,
talking together, and making sure that they work together to keep our communities safe.
That is a fantastic start to the year for National’s work on law and order, but,
actually, that is what this Government has been deliveri ng. We have seen a clamping
down—and there is legislation before this  House at the moment—on the criminal
activity of gangs. We are taking seriously the criminal activity of organised crime, both
in this country and internationally. The Prim e Minister himself has led the efforts to
clamp down on the production and sale of methamphetamine—that terrible, terrible
8026 General Debate 20 Feb 2013
drug that does such damage to our childre n. We have toughened sentences and we have
toughened bail, and we have abolished parole  for the worst repeat offenders. We have
put 600 extra police on the streets. The contrast with the previous Government, which
was transporting prisoners around in police vans, because it had taken so little—

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is important when we start
to look at the “pokies for convention cen tre” debacle to ask the question of why
transparency and accountability are important, be cause that is what this is about. At the
heart of a good democracy is th e notion that the exercise of  the people’s will will be
done in their interests—not in the interests of a small cabal, not in  the interests of a
particular business, and not in the interests of an individual, but in the interests of all the
people of New Zealand.
New Zealanders want simple things out of their Government. They want to be treated
fairly and they want to make sure that it is  accountable, that it is transparent, and that
they know what their elected representatives  are doing. Fundamentally, in this case the
New Zealand notion of a fair go has been broken. One submitter in this process was
treated more favourably than the others—a  fundamental breach of New Zealanders’
values of a fair go. A fair go was not presen t in this process. People were treated
differently. Skycity was treate d materially differently. It was not done in a transparent
or even-handed manner. They are not my words; they are the words of the Deputy
Auditor-General. This was not a fair process.  This was not a transparent process. This
was not an even-handed process, and that cu ts against the values of New Zealanders.
This Government should be ashamed about that.
The Prime Minister says he has been 100 percent vindicated. He has not. He has been
100 percent implicated in this case, because anyone who reads this report will see that
officials did not act in some vacuum. They  do not go off on a whim on these things.
They follow the lead of their Ministers. Th ey followed the lead of the Prime Minister
and they followed the lead of Steven Joy ce, the Minister for Economic Development.
That was what was happening here. Offici als have been hung out to dry by this
Government in this case, and the reality is that this was driven from the top. This was
driven from the Prime Minister. This phrase will become known for many years to
come: “the Skycity angle”. That is the phrase that John Key handwrote on a briefing
that he got from the Ministry of Tourism:  “close off the Skycity angle”. From that
moment onwards, officials went  down a path where Skycity got preferential treatment,
where other bidders were shut out of parts of  the process and transparency went out the
window.
The Prime Minister tipped the playing field here. The Prime Minister said to wait for
Skycity’s bid. The Prime Minister is the pers on who introduced th e idea of the “more
pokies for a convention centre” deal. He is donkey deep in this, but he denies it. He said
in June 2012: “my office has had no corr espondence, no discussions, no involvement”
in this matter. Stop the lying, Prime Minister —stop it. Tell the truth to New Zealanders
and tell them what actually happened here—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Our Standing Orders are
very clear. The deputy leader of the Labour Party cannot make those accusations of the
Rt Hon John Key.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Absolutely right. Would the member please withdraw that
comment.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I withdraw that comment. The Prime Minister has to start
telling the truth to New Zeala nders. The Prime Minister has to  start telling the truth to
New Zealanders about the involvement of his office. Here is what he also said: “…
Skycity will probably get a few more pokie m achines … at the margins.”—a few more
at the margins. Thirty percent more—30 percent more—pokie machines is what is
20 Feb 2013 General Debate 8027
happening there, and it is New Zealanders who will suffer. It is the terrible addition of
problem gambling that will be made worse by this, and the Prime Minister does not
care. He has got the deal. He is the one who tipped the playing field in favour of Skycity
and away from the other bidders. He is the one who led a non-transparent process. The 4
November dinner, the phrase “the Skycity  angle”, and where the Prime Minister
intervened are what New Zealanders will come to remember this sorry saga for.
I have no doubt that what we need now is for this process to be halted and started
again, so that New Zealanders can rebuild  their confidence in the operations of
government and we can be proud again of our transparency on the world stage. We will
lose from this as a country, because New Zealanders pride themselves on a democracy
where everybody gets a fair go. Under this G overnment, there is no fair go any longer.
It is its cronies and it is its mates. It is time for the Prime Minister to front up, tell the
truth about this, stop this deal, and give everybody a fair go.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I could hear the bottom of the
barrel scraping as the desperate deputy leader of the Labour Party gave that speech. Let
us cut to the chase. Labour made scurri lous allegations about the International
Convention Centre deal. The Opposition laid a complaint with the Auditor-General, and
the Auditor-General concluded that the Opposition got it wrong. If Opposition members
had an iota of decency or integrity, today’s speeches in  the House would have been
apologies from the Labour Party and the Green Party.
I am not going to get into a dissection dow n to the subparagraphs and sentences of
the Deputy Auditor-General’s re port. The Television New Zeal and headline said it all:
“Report clears Govt in SkyCity pokies deal”.
It speaks volumes that every one of the ma in dailies today gave greater prominence
to the resignation of Charles Chauvel fr om the Labour Party than to the Deputy
Auditor-General’s report on S kycity. What does that tell us? Well, remember that
Labour members had billed this Auditor-Gener al’s report as their big hit? This was
going to be the political game-changer for 2013. In stead, the story is that they have lost
one of their best brains.
Charles Chauvel can see the writing on the wall. Labour members are leaderless and
they are hopeless. They do not know what they stand for. They have resorted to
throwing mud, rather than actually dealing with the challenges facing New Zealand. The
fundamental problem for Labour on the issue of the International Convention Centre,
and more broadly, is simply one of credibility.
I have got a very simple question for the three Labour speakers who have spoken and
for the next Labour member to rise to th eir feet: why was it OK in 2001 for a Labour
Government to do a trade-off deal of 236 pokie machines for a $36 million convention
centre in Auckland? Where was Grant Robe rtson when that deal was done—with his
pious comments in the House this after noon? Where was David Shearer? Where were
the other Labour members? Where were the Greens? The Greens were propping up that
Government and not only did they not lay a complaint w ith the Auditor-General but
they did not speak an utteranc e over that arrangement. That reinforces that it is all
politics.
But there is a bigger problem for Labour. You see, David Shearer has been in charge
for over a year, and New Zealanders have no more idea today than then as to what he
stands for. As much as we have got from Mr Shearer is that he believes in hands-on
Government. Well, what the heck does that mean, when on all of the critical issues—
getting an international convention centre a nd the jobs from that, growing our oil and
gas industry, creating jobs in aquaculture, and creating and expanding irrigation to grow
our most important primary industry—Labour ha s said it is hands-off? All that exposes
8028 General Debate 20 Feb 2013
is that David Shearer’s fundamental lin e that Labour is goi ng to be a hands-on
Government is shallow words for a lack of policy.
There is another problem for Labour’s po sition on the Auditor-General’s report.
Labour members say that if there are any process problems—“process problems” is
what the Deputy Auditor-Gener al said—then it is cronyis m and corruption. Well, what
is happening next? There is another Auditor-G eneral’s report due next week. It is about
one of their colleagues, Mr Shane Jones. If  the Auditor-General finds that there are
“process problems” around the immigration issu es and the awarding of citizenship for a
certain gentleman, I wonder whether Labour members will be saying that is evidence of
“cronyism and corruption”—the words they used  today in the House. I suspect that Mr
Shearer and Mr Robertson will be singing a very different tune in the House next week.
I want to conclude with the facts. Labour  members went out and said the deal was
filthy. They said that it stunk. The Auditor-Ge neral’s office said it found no evidence to
suggest—in fact, it said these words: “nothing substantially wrong took place”. If
Labour members want any respect or credib ility, they should get to their feet and
apologise.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: This is the question, is it not? What does the
Labour Party stand for? What does the mode rn Labour Party stand for? The Labour
Party stands against jobs. The Labour Part y stands against investment. The Labour
Party stands against progress.  The Labour Party stands agai nst a convention centre in
Auckland. The Labour Party looks a gift-horse  in the mouth. But th e Labour Mayor of
Auckland stands for jobs, investment, grow th, and the Skycity convention centre. The
Labour Party spokesman for Auckland, the La bour Party mayor, says this is a good
idea. He cannot quite bring himself to say that publicly, but that is the code we get from
the town hall.
The new hands-on Labour Party over there—this is what it does—keeps its hands off
the jobs, it keeps its hands off investment, and it keeps its hands off sensible policy, but
it wants its hands on the levers of power. That is what it desperately wants. It wants its
hands on the levers of power. The reason I am here, Mr Speaker—and congratulations
on your first week in the job—is to keep the dispirited, the deluded, and the bewildered
on that side of the House. I am here to k eep these people—the di spirited, the deluded,
and the bewildered—on that side of the House.
Look how dispirited these turkeys are toda y, as they look forward to an early
Christmas. Look how dispirited they are. The fastest growing branch in the Labour
Party is the United Nations branch. It is the fastest growing branch. As the cruise ship
goes out of Auckland Harbour you can see th e Labour rats jumping into the tide and
swimming north towards New York—swimming north towards New York.
Anyway, we will not be losing any member s of the ACT Party caucus—we will not
be losing any members of the ACT Party cau cus. We stand our ground, we stand for
progress, we stand for investment, we stand for jobs, and we stand behind John Key and
his leadership of this count ry. Look, Labour members voted  three times to get their
present leader into the place of leadership, and he is sitting there like a possum caught in
the lights of “Hone” Carter’s Holden going up the Brynderwyns. That is how he looks
every day. The truth is that Labour is missing in action on the big issues.
The Labour Party has never been more unfit to govern this countr y in its history.
Labour is not serious about getting young people homeownership. What is the result?
What has it done? It has promised 10,000 houses—10,000 chicken coops—to be funded
by the next finance Minister, a Green member  of Parliament who says we should print
money to build 10,000 chicken coops for the chickens that  follow the Labour Party and
Green Party around the traps. What is the resu lt? Tens of thousands of New Zealanders
20 Feb 2013 General Debate 8029
are out of work because the Labour Part y believes in pricing young people off the
market.
This Labour Party—and I have been around a lot of Labour parties—should hang its
head in shame. It does not even have a front -bencher in the House. That is how serious
the Labour Party takes these debates. There is not anything about the Labour—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I believe it is outside the
Standing Orders to refer to the absence of members of the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is absolutely true. The member will refrain from referring to
the absence of any member.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: I ask people listening carefully on their crystal sets in the few
Labour constituencies that are left across Aotearoa to ask this question: is there anything
about the modern Labour Party and its lead ership, and is there anything about the
Greens—the old fogies and young dudes—that is going to give hope to this country? Is
there anything that they believ e in, and are prepared to bri ng to this House, that will
give hope to this country? That is why John Key and the National Party coalition—John
Key’s National and the ACT Party, sponsored  by the people of Epsom—remain well
ahead in the polls. We stand against the Labour Party ever getting its hands on the
levers of power.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Anyone listening to question time today
would have heard desperation from an O pposition whose own rats are leaving the
sinking ship. There are some substantial issues happening  in New Zealand at the
moment, but all David Shearer seems to care about is who had dinner with whom, and
all Metiria Turei cares about is  who lost sleep over what. Th e substantial issues in New
Zealand that we hear nothing about from the Opposition are about the jobs that are
being created. Did Opposition members ask any questions about that? Did they ask any
questions about the economic growth that is taking place in New Zealand? Did they ask
any questions about the infrastructure that is  being built, or the educational success of
New Zealand children? No, they did not—no, they did not.
Labour and the Greens are focu sed on the trivial, they ar e focused on gutter politics,
and they are focused on whining about things that they themselves did 10 years ago. Let
me read out a quote for the House, because I think it is quite a good one: “Here in New
Zealand it has been pleasing to  see continuing investment in  the quality of  our tourism
infrastructure.” and “In Auckland, Sky City has pumped $140 million into its new
Convention Centre,”. That, ladies and gen tlemen, came from Helen Clark. Helen Clark
did exactly the same type of deal that the Labour Party is complaining about now. Grant
Robertson wants to use a word, which in th is House he cannot us e, about John Key.
Well, I want to use a word that I am not supposed to use, and that is “hypocrisy”.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Helen Clark did exactly the same thing that Labour members are
complaining about right now. But the bottom line is that they made a serious accusation
against the Prime Minister of New Zeal and, and they were found dead wrong—they
were found absolutely wrong. Now it is time for Labour members to get to their feet and
for Green members to get to their feet and apologise, because they were found dead
wrong. The Deputy Auditor-General said that  there was absolutely no evidence to
suggest that the final decision to negotiate with Skycity was influenced by inappropriate
considerations. They were wrong, and it is time to apologise.
It is important to talk about what is actually important in this economy, and the
convention centre will be hugely benefici al for New Zealand—$90 million in annual
economic benefits, 1,000 jobs during constr uction, 800 jobs once it  is up and running.
Even the Labour Party Mayor of Auckland, wh om Labour is trying to disown over this
particular issue, supports the convention ce ntre. The Labour Part y does not stand for
8030 General Debate 20 Feb 2013
jobs. The Labour Party does not stand for economic growth. This convention centre that
the Labour Party is opposing will be hugely beneficial for Auckland and New Zealand,
but it is opposed to it.
The Labour Party should be talking about the big issues in this country, the big issues
that National members are focused on. We are focused on growth, we are focused on
jobs, and we are focused on infrastructure. When New Zealanders go to the polls next
year they will be asking themselves which party cares the most about their children’s
future. The Labour Party opposes every pro- jobs policy that this Government has
introduced. The Greens are interested just in  wrapping New Zealand up in red tape and
printing more money.
Well, National has got a good story to tell in those areas. In jobs, 65,000 new jobs
have been created in the past 3 years, and more than 13,000 jobs have been created with
the 90-day trial. We hear about lay-offs. Th e Labour Party wants to talk about lay-offs.
It wants to talk about Main zeal Property and Construction  and it wants to talk about
Solid Energy, but it never wants to hear about the good-news stories—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Tell us about the people who have given up looking for work
because there’s no hope under this Government.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: —such as 1,000 new jobs from the Waterview Connection
motorway. Listen up, Mr Lees-Galloway; if you listened for a second, you would get
some facts into your brain. There are nearly  2,000 jobs from the ultra-fast broadband
roll-out, and 1,000 jobs for Wiri Prison.
I heard during question time from the good Mi nister of Corrections about the global
positioning system bracelets that she is in troducing. I think, actually, David Shearer
would like to have some of those for his own caucus, and there could be a proximity
meter next to David Cunliffe’s office so when Labour Party memb ers go next to his
office to become the next abstention in th eir next vote, David Sh earer knows all about
it.
We are focused on economic growth as well. This economy is growing by 2.5
percent. Labour would love to knock us down, but the good-news story, the facts out
there, is that this economy is growing. After-tax wages are up 20 percent since 2008—
over twice the rate of inflation. Household di sposable income has increased almost one-
third in 4 years. We never hear about th e good-news stories from the Labour Party,
because it does not care. It does not care about jobs, it does not care about growth, and it
does not care about infrastructure. Those me mbers need to stand up and say sorry for
their accusations. They were found absolutely wrong, and it is time they got to their feet
and said so.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call in this
general debate. Could I recommend this book, the Deputy Auditor-Gen eral’s report, to
the National Party members? It is worth reading. Instead of just repeating the lies that
have been presented to them in their resear ch notes and then reading them out to the
House, read this report and hang your heads in  shame. This is not what New Zealanders
expect of their Government, let alone of their Prime Minister.
I do not mind if the National Party wants to do  a lot of legislation that I do not agree
with, and I do not mind if it wants to introduce  policies that make me feel ill when I
look at the impact on people who live in my co mmunities, because that is its right as a
democratically elected Government in our c ountry. It was elected to implement what I
think are bad policies, but we are not part of the Government. We will be in 18 months’
time. But this is not about bad policies. Th is is not about a democratically elected
Government introducing legislation that is not popular but that it  is mandated to do.
This is about a shonky, dirty d eal, and it is about that far away from being corrupt. And
that is what the Deputy Auditor-General says in the report.
20 Feb 2013 General Debate 8031

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: No it’s not.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Sam Lotu-Iiga will not have r ead it. I know he will not have
read it.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: Have you read it all?

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I absolutely have, and I could quote quite a lot of it. The
interesting thing that the National Party ha s not mentioned in this debate is that,
actually, it is obvious from this re port that the Skycity team always intended to build a
convention centre. That is what it wanted to do. So not only have we got an organisation
that wanted to do a convention centre but we have got the Government personally
involved, with Ministers having meetings and dinners and saying: “We know you were
going to do that. It’s all part of your legitimate business plan. But what we want to do is
make it sweeter and easier for you.”

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: Rubbish.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It is bribing an organisation to do something that, actually, it
was going to do anyway. Sam Lotu-Iiga says it is rubbish—he has just confirmed that
he has not read the report. It says in here  that in 2009 Skycity told officials that it
wanted to build a new convention centre.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What page? Quote the page.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Read the report, lazy member of Parliament, read the report. It
says that Skycity wanted—

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I would like the member
to sit down while I give my point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes, and I will hear the point of order. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: Excuse me.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Just get on with the point of order, please.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: I take offence to that member  calling me lazy, because those
who know me know I am not lazy. That member should quote the page of the report she
is referring to. If she says she has read the report—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a robust debating chamber. There will always be
comments made about members. I do not think that is one that the member should have
taken offence at. I am going to ask the member to continue.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Th e member has actually just
confirmed how lazy he is, because he wants me to look up the page in the report that I
was quoting. You cannot get much lazier than  asking a member of another party to look
up a report. It is gobsmacking.

items.speaker: Let me raise a few quotes
items.text: “Ministry officials were aware that SkyCity had expressed
an interest in extending its existing c onvention centre across Federal Street or
developing a new centre on land it owned in Hobson Street. This awareness arose from
communications between Auckland-based Mini stry officials and SkyCity during April
and May 2009.” Skycity wanted to build the convention centre. It needed no
Government assistance. It was always going to  do it. It was always going to pay for it.
What the Prime Minister has done is expos e his shonky deal, his n eed to be snuggling
up to business, in a way that is that far aw ay from corruption. It is the worst report I
have seen in my time in Parliament as to  the behaviour of members of Parliament and
Ministers.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: Quote the page. Quote the page if you know it.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Lazy personified. John Armstrong, in his comment this
morning in the New Zealand Herald, said that the report show ed that we are verging on
banana republic kind  of stuff without the bananas.  He said: “In other words, no
corruption. Or at least none that could be found.”, and that the process had been “neither
transparent nor even-handed … Things got so bad”—he reported, and it is in the
8032 General Debate 20 Feb 2013
report—“that some officials expressed concern to superiors that proper procedures were
not being followed.”
On every page of this report we see John Ke y’s statement that there is nothing to see
made a lie of. Every single page has a damn ing comment. Steven Joyce gets the spin
going, and his trained seals in the National Party repeat it. Read the report and hang
your heads in shame.

items.speaker: Dr JACKIE BLUE
items.text: I am pleased to speak in the general debate. Thank
goodness, I say—thank goodness we have got a Pr ime Minister who is focused on the
big picture: economic development, jo bs, and boosting our economy. We are not
distracted by the sideshows. We have had a challenging few years. There is no question
about that. But that is why the economy must be front and centre stage, and that is why
we are determined to continue with the economic growth that we have made strong
foundations for over the last 4 years.
We are doing quite well compared with othe r countries. We are re ally fortunate. We
